screens.title: Implementing Basic Movement & Seeking Behaviors
screens.subtitle: Turning vectors into believable AI motion in Unity

narration.text: In this chapter we'll make AI agents move and react in 3D using the same math that underlies every game world. You'll learn how a Vector3 describes position and direction, why normalizing a vector matters, and how to use delta time so movement is consistent across frame rates. We'll practice both direct movement and Unity helper functions that help avoid overshoot or smooth motion. You will see how seeking and fleeing differ only by vector sign, and how rotation choices affect character stability when the target is above or below. We then add simple obstacle avoidance using raycasts and LayerMasks so agents see and steer around blockers. Along the way you'll get concrete code examples you can drop into a cube or capsule, plus a short hands-on activity to test avoidance behavior in the Scene view. By the end, you'll be able to create a cube that seeks a sphere, turns smoothly, and avoids simple obstacles — and you'll know what to check when things go wrong. Ready to build dependable movement for your AI?

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Use normalized direction vectors, Time.deltaTime, and Unity helpers to move and rotate agents reliably; add raycast checks and LayerMasks for simple obstacle avoidance.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These objectives guide hands-on practice and diagnostics. First, you will apply vector mathematics to control an agent's movement and direction in three-dimensional space. That means calculating vectors, normalizing them, and using magnitudes to reason about speed. Second, you'll implement seeking and fleeing behaviors using both manual vector updates and Unity helpers like MoveTowards and Lerp, and learn when each is appropriate. Third, you will design basic obstacle avoidance with raycasts, using layered detection to ignore irrelevant objects. Fourth, you'll ensure movement is frame-rate independent with Time. deltaTime and learn common debugging checks for movement and rotation issues. Each objective includes a practical example: for vector math you'll move a cube to a sphere; for seeking and fleeing you'll toggle a boolean to invert direction; for obstacle avoidance you'll cast forward rays and rotate when blocked; and for frame-rate independence you'll compare movement at varying fixed and variable frame rates. These skills matter because they make AI predictable, testable, and robust on different hardware. Can you see how each objective builds toward believable agent behavior?

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Skills Breakdown
screens.subtitle: Concrete skills and why they matter

narration.text: Now let's break the objectives into concrete skills you can test quickly. Skill one is calculating and normalizing a direction vector so the agent moves at a predictable rate. A quick check is to print the vector’s magnitude and confirm it becomes one after normalization. Skill two is implementing seeking and fleeing: toggle a boolean to invert the movement vector and watch the agent flip between approach and retreat. Skill three is using MoveTowards for consistent, no-overshoot motion and experimenting with Lerp to observe the slowing approach it produces. Skill four is setting up a forward raycast, assigning a LayerMask to only detect obstacles, and using Debug. DrawRay to watch hits change color. Each skill is testable: change speed, change ray length, and observe behavior. These are practical checks you can run inside Play mode. Practice them until you can explain why each change produced the agent’s new movement. That explanation is the sign of real understanding.

narration.text: Vector mathematics is the foundation of any movement system in three-dimensional games. A Vector3 either locates a point in space or encodes a direction and magnitude. When you want an agent to move toward a target you subtract the agent’s position from the target’s position to produce a direction vector. That raw difference encodes both how far and where to move. Normalizing that vector removes magnitude information and leaves only direction, which is essential when you want movement at a specific speed. For example, if a cube at position A wants to reach a sphere at position B, compute the difference, set the vertical component to zero if you want ground-only movement, then normalize. Multiply the resulting unit vector by a speed scalar and Time. deltaTime to produce a displacement. A common misconception is that normalizing is optional; skipping it causes movement speed to vary with distance because the magnitude of the difference carries through. Another subtle point: when the agent is close to the target, magnitude becomes small and floating point noise can make the agent jitter; clamp small magnitudes or use MoveTowards to avoid overshoot. To check your math, log magnitudes before and after normalizing and watch them converge to one. Can you explain why normalization gives you speed control independent of distance?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Subtract positions to get a direction vector, set y to zero for horizontal movement, normalize to get a unit direction, then scale by speed and Time.deltaTime.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Vector Mathematics
Concept Cards
Position vs Direction
A position marks a point. A direction is the difference between two positions and shows where to go.
Normalization
Converting to a unit vector preserves direction while removing magnitude, enabling fixed-speed movement.
Magnitude and Clamping
Very small magnitudes near the target can cause jitter; clamp or use MoveTowards to stop cleanly.
Concrete Example
Imagine an agent at x equals zero z equals zero and a target at x equals ten z equals zero. The raw difference is ten along x. Normalizing produces one along x, so multiplying by speed will move the agent exactly at the chosen speed rather than ten times that speed. If you forgot to normalize, your agent would move faster the further it starts from the target, which usually feels wrong.
Key Takeaway

Normalize direction vectors to separate direction from distance and keep motion predictable.

Common Mistake
Not zeroing the vertical component leads to unintended vertical movement when the target is above or below the agent.

screens.title: Frame-Rate Independent Movement
screens.subtitle: Why Time.deltaTime matters and how to use it

narration.text: Frame-rate independence ensures your AI moves the same way regardless of hardware. Time. deltaTime represents the time in seconds since the previous frame, so multiplying any per-frame delta by it converts per-frame changes into per-second rates. The typical flow is: compute a normalized direction, multiply by a speed in units per second, then multiply by Time. deltaTime to get the per-frame displacement, and finally add that to the agent’s position. A common test is to run the game with different target frame rates or in the editor's slow motion and verify the agent covers the same distance per real second. One misconception is to use Time. deltaTime twice, or to leave it out entirely. Using it twice will under-scale movement at low frame rates; leaving it out makes speed depend on frame rate. Another consideration is using fixed update loops for physics-driven movement, but for transform position updates Time. deltaTime in Update is correct. In short, treat speed as a per-second value and scale by delta time to compute the per-frame step. Try changing speed and observe that distance covered per second scales linearly while frame rate changes do not affect motion.

keyIdea.title: Process
keyIdea.text: Compute normalized direction, multiply by speed (units/sec), scale by Time.deltaTime, then apply to transform.position for consistent motion.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Frame-Rate Independence
Step-by-Step
1. Compute direction
target minus agent, zero y if needed, normalize.
2. Scale speed
Multiply unit direction by speed measured in units per second.
3. Apply delta time
Multiply by Time.deltaTime to compute per-frame displacement.
4. Update position
Add displacement to transform.position or use MoveTowards for clamping.
Concrete Example
If speed is five units per second and Time.deltaTime equals 0.02 seconds, the agent moves 0.1 units this frame. If the frame time changes to 0.0167, the per-frame step adapts so the per-second distance remains near five. This makes behavior predictable when testing on different machines or when game load spikes.
Key Takeaway

Always treat speed as units per second and multiply by Time.deltaTime for each frame update to keep motion consistent.

Common Mistake
Using Time.deltaTime in FixedUpdate incorrectly or omitting it entirely causes inconsistent speeds; choose the right loop for your implementation.

screens.title: Seeking and Fleeing Behavior
screens.subtitle: Implement approach and retreat using direction vectors

narration.text: Seeking behavior is simply the agent choosing to move toward a target, while fleeing is moving away from it. The implementation difference is small but conceptually important: compute the direction from agent to target, optionally flatten the vertical axis, then normalize. For seeking you apply the direction; for fleeing you apply the negative of that direction. In practice you also control when to switch behaviors — for example, flee when the player comes within a danger radius, and seek otherwise. A common implementation error is to forget to normalize before applying speed, causing the agent to move faster when more distant. Another pitfall is using rotation methods that immediately snap orientation when you want a smooth turn. You can test behavior by toggling a boolean in the Inspector and observing the agent switch between approach and retreat. A concrete scenario: create a cube as AI and a sphere as the player. When the sphere is farther than a threshold, the cube seeks; when inside the threshold it flees. This produces emergent and testable behavior with very few lines of code. How would you combine this with obstacle avoidance so the agent flees but still avoids walls?

keyIdea.title: Claim
keyIdea.text: Seeking uses the normalized direction to target; fleeing uses the negative of that vector. Toggle based on conditions to create reactive behaviors.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Seeking & Fleeing
Behavior Cards
Seek
Apply normalized direction toward target, multiply by speed and delta time.
Flee
Invert the normalized direction to move away from the target. Use conditions to switch modes.
Condition Example
If distance to target is less than a threshold, set isFleeing true; otherwise false.
Concrete Scenario
A guard cube seeks the player until the player gets too close, then flees back to a safe distance. Implementing this requires only a distance check and toggling whether movement uses direction or its inverse. Pair this with raycast checks to maintain collision-safe fleeing.
Key Takeaway

Seek and flee share the same vector math; invert the direction to change intent and add condition checks to switch behaviors.

Check Your Understanding
How would you make the agent slowly switch from seeking to fleeing instead of toggling instantly? Consider blending directions over time.

screens.title: Vector3.MoveTowards vs Vector3.Lerp
screens.subtitle: When to use MoveTowards for constant speed and Lerp for smoothing

narration.text: MoveTowards and Lerp are useful helpers, but they behave differently. MoveTowards moves the current point toward the target by a maximum distance per call. That makes it ideal when you want guaranteed constant or clamped travel and to avoid overshooting the target. Lerp returns a point between two vectors based on an interpolation factor between zero and one. When you use Lerp with a small factor multiplied by delta time, you create a smoothing effect where the object decays exponentially toward the target and slows as it approaches. This smoothing can look more natural for some animations, but it does not maintain a constant speed. A frequent misconception is to treat Lerp as a constant-speed interpolator; it is not, unless you manually compute the t parameter over a fixed duration. In practice, prefer MoveTowards for navigation and collision-sensitive movement, and use Lerp for soft follow cameras or smoothing values. To compare them, set an initial distance and observe MoveTowards covering equal steps until it stops, while Lerp quickly reduces distance then asymptotically approaches the target. Which behavior fits your gameplay depends on whether constant speed or smooth slowing looks better for your agent.

keyIdea.title: Comparison
keyIdea.text: Use MoveTowards for constant-speed, non-overshooting movement; use Lerp for smoothing and exponential approach but not constant velocity.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › MoveTowards vs Lerp
Side-by-Side
MoveTowards
Moves by a max delta per frame. Prevents overshoot and maintains predictable step sizes when scaled by delta time.
Lerp
Interpolates toward the target based on a factor. Produces exponential decay when used with delta time and smoothing factors.
Practical rule: use MoveTowards for navigation and collision-critical movement, Lerp for smoothing and visual polish where constant speed is not required.
Concrete Test
Place an agent ten units from a target. With MoveTowards and max delta two, it will march two units per frame interval until arrival. With Lerp and factor 0.1 times delta time, it will cover a large portion early and then slow, never exactly reaching the target in finite frames without special handling.
Key Takeaway

Choose MoveTowards for consistent speed and collision safety; choose Lerp for smoothing and a gentle slow-down approach.

screens.title: Reading the AISimpleMovement Script
screens.subtitle: Understand the provided example step by step

narration.text: Let's walk through the example AISimpleMovement script and explain how each part contributes to movement and avoidance. The script exposes public fields for the target Transform, movement and rotation speeds, the avoidance distance, and the obstacle LayerMask so you can tune behavior from the Inspector. In Update it first checks for a valid target to avoid null reference issues. It computes a direction to the target, zeros the vertical component so the agent stays grounded, and normalizes to get a unit direction. The script demonstrates a forward raycast to detect obstacles within the avoidance distance and sets an avoidance direction if one is found; the simple example rotates the forward vector by a fixed angle to steer away. After computing the final movement direction the script applies a frame-rate independent position change by multiplying by moveSpeed and Time. deltaTime. Rotation uses Quaternion. LookRotation to create the desired orientation and Quaternion. Slerp to smoothly blend the current rotation toward that orientation. Common mistakes include forgetting to set the LayerMask correctly or neglecting to flatten the y component, which causes unintended vertical motion. Reading and stepping through this script in Play mode while watching Debug. DrawRay will make the logic clear. What one change would you try first to make avoidance more robust?

keyIdea.title: Code structure
keyIdea.text: Public tuning fields, direction math, raycast avoidance, frame-rate independent movement, and smooth rotation via quaternions form the main structure.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › AISimpleMovement Walkthrough
Key Sections
  • Public fields: target, speeds, avoidance distance, LayerMask for runtime tuning.
  • Target check: early return if null to avoid errors.
  • Direction math: subtract, zero y, normalize.
  • Raycast avoidance: forward ray with hit check and alternate steering.
  • Movement and rotation: position update with delta time and slerp for rotation.
Pro Tip
Use Debug.DrawRay to see the avoidance ray change color on hit; tune avoidance distance until the agent reliably steers clear of colliders.
Code Panel (Excerpt)
// Example excerpt: compute direction, check raycast, move and rotate
Vector3 directionToTarget = target.position - transform.position;
directionToTarget.y = 0; // horizontal movement
directionToTarget.Normalize();

// Raycast forward for avoidance
if (Physics.Raycast(transform.position, transform.forward, out hit, obstacleAvoidanceDistance, obstacleLayer)) {
    // Avoidance: rotate forward by a fixed angle
    avoidanceDirection = Quaternion.Euler(0,45,0) * transform.forward;
}

// Apply movement
transform.position += finalMovementDirection * moveSpeed * Time.deltaTime;

// Smooth rotation
Quaternion targetRotation = Quaternion.LookRotation(directionToTarget);
transform.rotation = Quaternion.Slerp(transform.rotation, targetRotation, rotationSpeed * Time.deltaTime);
Note: This panel shows the logical flow. Keep code in the editor and use Debug.DrawRay during Play mode to visualize results.

screens.title: Rotation Techniques & Stability
screens.subtitle: LookAt vs Quaternion.LookRotation and using Slerp for smooth turns

narration.text: Rotation choices affect how natural the agent appears and whether it avoids sudden snaps or unwanted tilting. transform. LookAt is a convenient single-call solution that points the forward axis to the target position, but it can cause unwanted rotations if the target is directly above or below, or if the object has complex child hierarchies that expect a different up axis. A more controlled approach is to compute a rotation with Quaternion. LookRotation using the movement direction, then smooth the transition using Quaternion. Slerp. Slerp interpolates on the sphere of rotations, producing a natural constant angular velocity blend that avoids abrupt changes. One misconception is that Slerp always produces the same perceived speed of turn; the perceived speed depends on the rotation difference and the interpolation factor. For characters that must remain upright, build your direction vector with a zeroed vertical component before using LookRotation so pitch changes are suppressed. In practice set rotationSpeed to a tuned value and observe rotation in Play mode. If you see sudden flips when the target crosses overhead, clamp or adjust the up vector and use Slerp to blend. How might you combine Slerp with obstacle avoidance so the agent both steers and faces its movement direction smoothly?

keyIdea.title: Rotation guidance
keyIdea.text: Prefer Quaternion.LookRotation plus Slerp for controlled, smooth orientation; zero vertical components to keep characters upright and avoid tilting.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Rotation & Stability
Rotation Patterns
transform.LookAt
Instantly orient forward axis to target. Quick and simple, but can tilt objects and cause snaps.
Quaternion.LookRotation + Slerp
Compute desired rotation from movement direction, then smoothly interpolate for controlled turning.
Keep Upright
Zero the vertical component of direction before look rotation to avoid pitching when target is above or below.
Concrete Tip
If your agent snaps when the player passes overhead, build the rotation from a horizontal direction vector and then Slerp towards that rotation. This preserves upright posture and yields a natural turn. Tune rotationSpeed in small increments while watching tuning results in Play mode.
Key Takeaway

Use quaternion-based rotations with smoothing for stable, natural orientation behavior and prevent gimbal-like tilting by controlling the up axis.

screens.title: Raycast-Based Obstacle Avoidance
screens.subtitle: Detecting obstacles and choosing a steer direction

narration.text: A basic but effective avoidance technique uses raycasts to detect obstacles ahead and steer the agent to a clear path. The minimal flow is: cast a ray forward from the agent, test if it hits within an avoidance distance using a LayerMask, and if it does, compute a rotated alternative direction and use that to move instead of the direct direction to target. In the simplest example the script rotates the forward vector by a fixed angle to the right; more robust approaches check both sides by casting additional rays at angles and choose the first clear path. Important practical notes: set the LayerMask to include only obstacles you want to avoid, so you don't accidentally detect the player or other agents unless desired. Use Debug. DrawRay to see hits and misses in Scene view; change the ray color to red on hit and green when clear to speed debugging. A frequent error is forgetting to normalize the avoidance direction before applying speed, which produces inconsistent steering. Another is casting from the wrong origin — cast slightly above the ground if your AI's origin is at the mesh pivot to avoid missing low obstacles. How would you extend this approach to detect obstacles of varying heights?

keyIdea.title: Avoidance pattern
keyIdea.text: Raycast forward using an obstacle LayerMask; on hit, rotate forward or cast side rays to find a clear steering direction, then normalize and move.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Raycast Avoidance
Avoidance Steps
  1. Cast a forward ray with Physics.Raycast from the agent origin.
  2. Use a LayerMask to filter only relevant colliders.
  3. On hit, try rotated forward directions or cast side rays to find a clear path.
  4. Normalize the chosen direction and move using speed times delta time.
Debugging Tip
Switch LayerMask in the Inspector to include or exclude layers and watch Debug.DrawRay change color when a hit occurs.
Concrete Example
If a forward ray hits within three units, rotate the forward vector by forty five degrees and test that rotated vector. If that rotated ray is clear, use it. If not, rotate the other way and test again. This reactive approach keeps the AI moving instead of stopping or penetrating colliders. For taller obstacles, cast from a higher origin or use multiple vertical rays to detect variety in height.
Key Takeaway

Raycasts give a simple reactive method to avoid obstacles; combine angled checks and LayerMasks for better results.

screens.title: Extending Avoidance: Multiple Rays & Steering
screens.subtitle: From a simple right turn to checking multiple angles for a clear path

narration.text: A single fixed-angle avoidance can work as a quick demo but fails in complex scenes. To improve reliability, cast multiple rays at varying angles and choose the clearest option. For example, after a forward hit, cast rays at thirty, sixty, and ninety degrees left and right. Evaluate which rays return no hit within the avoidance distance and select the best steering vector, typically the first clear side ray or the one with the greatest free distance. Normalize that steering vector before applying movement. This approach reduces the chance of getting stuck in tight corridors. You can also weight candidate directions by how well they align with the original direction so the agent prefers paths closer to the target. Remember to respect the LayerMask and to cast from a sensible height above ground if obstacles vary in height. A common misconception is that more rays always equal better behavior; in practice balance detection accuracy with performance by limiting the number of rays and checking only when needed. Try tuning the number and angle of side rays and observe how the AI navigates a tight obstacle cluster. Which trade-off would you accept: slower checks or smoother navigation?

keyIdea.title: Steering improvement
keyIdea.text: Cast side rays at multiple angles and select the first clear or best-weighted direction to create robust steering in cluttered environments.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Multi-Ray Steering
Multi-ray Strategy
Cast rays at several angles when an obstacle is detected. Choose the first clear ray or compute a score that prefers directions closest to the original path. Normalize and move along the chosen vector. Tune ray count and angles to balance CPU work and navigation quality.
Angle Examples
Check 30°, 60°, and 90° left/right and choose the most suitable clear path.
Weighted Selection
Prefer directions that minimize deviation from the original target direction to keep the agent efficient.
Performance Note
Only perform the full sweep when a forward ray hits. Keep ray count moderate — three to five side checks are often sufficient. Use LayerMask to minimize unnecessary physics checks.
Common Mistake

Casting too many rays every frame can burden performance; trigger additional checks only when necessary.

screens.title: LayerMask and Debugging Movement Issues
screens.subtitle: Common problems and how to diagnose them

narration.text: When AI walks through objects, or ignores obstacles, LayerMask mistakes are often the culprit. LayerMask tells Physics queries which layers to include. If your obstacles sit on a layer excluded from the mask, raycasts will act as if those colliders do not exist. Always verify LayerMask assignments in the Inspector and use temporary visual cues like Debug. DrawRay to confirm the ray's path and whether a hit is reported. Another common issue is using the wrong origin or direction for the ray; confirm you cast from the agent’s collision origin and that the direction aligns with transform. forward or the computed movement direction. Movement jitter often stems from applying tiny residual displacements when very close to the target; fix this by clamping small magnitudes or snapping to the target when within a small threshold. Also check for double updates when both a physics system and manual transform changes affect the same object. A practical debugging sequence is: confirm target reference, visualize raycasts, log hit results and layers, then incrementally adjust ray length and LayerMask. Which of these checks would you add to your debug checklist first?

keyIdea.title: Debug checklist
keyIdea.text: Verify target assignment, correct LayerMask, ray origin and direction, and clamp small displacements; use Debug.DrawRay for visual confirmation.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › LayerMask & Debugging
Common Issues
  • Raycast ignores obstacles because LayerMask excludes their layer.
  • Raycast origin is inside another collider or below ground, causing missed hits.
  • Movement jitter near target due to tiny residual displacements.
  • Conflicting updates between physics and direct transform changes.
Debug Sequence
1. Confirm targetTransform is assigned and not null.
2. Visualize rays with Debug.DrawRay and check colors change on hits.
3. Log RaycastHit.collider and verify the collider's layer and tag.
4. Adjust LayerMask in Inspector to include obstacle layers only.
Key Takeaway

Systematic checks with visual feedback quickly pinpoint most movement and detection issues; tune LayerMask and origins first.

screens.title: Hands-on: Build SeekAndAvoidAI
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step lab to implement and test seeking with avoidance

narration.text: This hands-on activity walks you through creating SeekAndAvoidAI so you can see the concepts in action. Start by creating a C sharp script with public fields for targetTransform, moveSpeed, rotationSpeed, avoidanceRayLength, avoidanceTurnAngle, and obstacleLayer. Attach it to a cube and assign a sphere as the target. In Update, confirm the target is set. Compute the direction vector, flatten the vertical axis, and normalize. Cast a forward ray using the avoidanceRayLength and obstacleLayer. If the ray hits, set the movement direction to a rotated forward vector using the avoidanceTurnAngle; otherwise use the direction to the target. Apply movement by adding the final direction times moveSpeed times Time. deltaTime to transform. position. For rotation, compute a look rotation toward the finalDirection and use Quaternion. Slerp to blend rotationSpeed times delta time. Add OnDrawGizmosSelected to visualize the agent and target, and use Debug. DrawRay to color the ray red on hit and green when clear. Iterate on avoidanceTurnAngle and ray length to observe how the agent navigates obstacles. This active cycle of change and observation is the fastest way to internalize these movement patterns. What parameter will you tune first to get smooth navigation?

keyIdea.title: Lab goal
keyIdea.text: Implement SeekAndAvoidAI with public tuning fields, raycast avoidance, frame-rate independent movement, and visual debugging to test behavior.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Hands-on: SeekAndAvoidAI
Lab Steps
  1. Create SeekAndAvoidAI script and add public fields for tuning.
  2. In Update verify targetTransform is assigned before proceeding.
  3. Compute direction, zero the y component, normalize.
  4. Cast forward ray and on hit rotate forward by avoidanceTurnAngle or cast side rays to find a clear path.
  5. Move using finalDirection times moveSpeed times Time.deltaTime and rotate with Slerp.
  6. Use Debug.DrawRay and OnDrawGizmosSelected for visualization and tuning.
Testing Notes
Place a few cube obstacles on a dedicated layer, assign that layer to obstacleLayer, and watch how tuning changes behavior in Play mode.
Starter Template (Visual)
// SeekAndAvoidAI template fields
public Transform targetTransform;
public float moveSpeed = 4f;
public float rotationSpeed = 7f;
public float avoidanceRayLength = 2.5f;
public float avoidanceTurnAngle = 60f;
public LayerMask obstacleLayer;

// In Update: compute direction, cast ray, choose finalDirection, move and rotate.
This template summarizes the fields and flow. Implement logic carefully and use the Inspector to tune values while observing Scene view rays.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 1
screens.subtitle: What to remember and why it matters

narration.text: Let's summarize the most important ideas from this chapter. First, Vector Mathematics: subtracting positions gives a direction vector, normalizing keeps movement speed independent of distance, and zeroing the vertical component constrains agents to the ground. Second, Seeking and Fleeing: they are the same math with inverted direction; toggle behavior to create reactive AI. Third, Time. deltaTime: always treat speed as units per second and multiply by delta time to compute per-frame displacement so behavior is consistent across frame rates. These three form the backbone of predictable movement. Practice them together: compute direction, normalize, scale by speed, multiply by delta time, and apply position or MoveTowards. Each step reduces a source of bugs and makes tuning more straightforward. Repeat these checks until they become second nature for working with AI motion.

keyIdea.title: Remember
keyIdea.text: Direction math, flipping for flee, and scaling by Time.deltaTime are the core pillars of consistent AI movement.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Key Concepts — Part 1
Vector Mathematics
Positions and directions are Vector3 values; normalize for unit direction and control speed separately.
Seeking & Fleeing
Seek uses the direction vector; flee uses the inverse. Use conditions to switch behaviors dynamically.
Time.deltaTime
Scale per-second speeds by delta time to compute accurate per-frame movement and ensure consistent results across devices.
Summary Takeaway
Combine direction math, delta time scaling, and clear decision rules to build reliable and testable AI movement systems.

narration.text: Finish with the remaining essentials. First, MoveTowards versus Lerp: MoveTowards yields constant steps and prevents overshoot, while Lerp is best for smoothing and creating an exponential approach. Second, rotation: prefer Quaternion. LookRotation with Quaternion. Slerp to avoid instant snaps and maintain smooth orientation; zero vertical components when you need upright characters. Third, raycast-based avoidance and LayerMask: cast rays forward and at angles, filter with LayerMask to detect only intended obstacles, and use Debug. DrawRay to visualize hits. These ideas complete the practical tool set for simple AI locomotion: controlled movement, smooth facing, and reactive steering. When debugging, follow a short checklist: verify target assignment, inspect LayerMask settings, visualize rays, and clamp small displacements near the destination. Together these concepts make agents that move believably and robustly in many scenes. What will you try adjusting first to improve your agent's behavior?

keyIdea.title: Remember
keyIdea.text: Use MoveTowards for precise motion, Slerp for smooth rotation, and layered raycasts with Debug.DrawRay for robust, debuggable avoidance.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Key Concepts — Part 2
MoveTowards vs Lerp
Choose MoveTowards for constant, clamped motion; choose Lerp for smoothing where gradual slowing is desirable.
Quaternion Rotation
Slerp between current and target rotations to create smooth, natural facing behavior without abrupt snaps.
Raycasting & LayerMask
Use LayerMask to target specific colliders and cast multiple rays when needed; visualize with Debug.DrawRay for fast debugging.
Final Takeaway
Combine reliable vector math, time scaling, appropriate helper functions, and careful raycasts with layered detection to build predictable and debuggable AI movement systems.
